query: Eutectic high-entropy alloys contain dual-phase lamellar colonies with numerous internal boundaries, where microcracking can initiate and lead to catastrophic damage during room-temperature tensile deformation. Conventional processing commonly raises strength at the expense of ductility, while the wide range of previously proposed microstructural-design and processing strategies has not eliminated room-temperature brittleness and limited tensile ductility. Under these constraints, what single intervention could improve both strength and room-temperature tensile ductility? State one testable hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts outcomes relative to the unmodified lamellar-colony baseline, defines its boundary conditions, cites supporting prior evidence, and proposes an experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: A tailored low‐temperature annealing treatment that promotes in situ interfacial segregation and ordering at the lamellar boundaries will simultaneously improve both the strength and the room-temperature tensile ductility of eutectic high-entropy alloys by reinforcing the interface cohesion and retarding microcrack initiation.
generation.material_initial_state: Eutectic high-entropy alloy with dual-phase lamellar colonies characterized by numerous internal boundaries prone to microcrack initiation under tensile loading at room temperature.
generation.intervention: Apply a controlled low‐temperature annealing process designed to induce selective solute segregation and ordering at the lamellar interfaces.
generation.conditions: Room-temperature tensile deformation; starting from a conventionally cast EHEA with a fine lamellar microstructure.
generation.structural_mediator: Enhanced interfacial cohesion due to in situ segregation and ordering at the lamellar boundaries.
generation.mechanism: The annealing treatment enables certain alloying elements to diffusively segregate and order at the phase boundaries, thereby strengthening the interfaces. This improved cohesion delays the nucleation and propagation of microcracks, leading to a more uniform strain distribution during tensile deformation.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to untreated samples, the treated EHEA is expected to exhibit higher yield and fracture strengths along with improved elongation at room temperature, reflecting a simultaneous enhancement in strength and ductility.
generation.baseline: As-cast EHEA with a fine lamellar microstructure whose numerous internal boundaries serve as initiation sites for microcracking, limiting its ductility despite high strength.
generation.boundary: The improvement is contingent upon annealing conditions that are optimized to induce beneficial interfacial modifications without causing detrimental phase coarsening or unwanted changes in the bulk microstructure. The effect may vary with alloy composition and precise thermal parameters.
generation.uncertainty: The magnitude of the improvements in mechanical properties is dependent on the specific annealing temperature, duration, and alloy diffusion kinetics, and there is a risk of over-annealing leading to phase degradation instead of beneficial interface strengthening.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of EHEA samples: one set receives the tailored low-temperature annealing treatment, and the control set remains as-cast. Both sets should be subjected to standardized room-temperature tensile testing as well as detailed microstructural analysis focusing on the lamellar interfaces.
measurements: Transmission electron microscopy (TEM) and energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS) analysis of the interfaces for evidence of segregation and ordering
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the annealed samples do not exhibit statistically significant improvements in both tensile strength and ductility relative to the as-cast controls, or if microstructural analysis fails to reveal enhanced interfacial segregation/ordering, then the hypothesis must be rejected.

cited_evidence.text: High-entropy alloys (HEAs) can have either high strength or high ductility, and a simultaneous achievement of both still constitutes a tough challenge. The inferior castability and compositional segregation of HEAs are also obstacles for their technological applications. To tackle these problems, here we proposed a novel strategy to design HEAs using the eutectic alloy concept, i.e. to achieve a microstructure composed of alternating soft fcc and hard bcc phases. As a manifestation of this concept, an AlCoCrFeNi2.1 (atomic portion) eutectic high-entropy alloy (EHEA) was designed. The as-cast EHEA possessed a fine lamellar fcc/B2 microstructure, and showed an unprecedented combination of high tensile ductility and high fracture strength at room temperature. The excellent mechanical properties could be kept up to 700°C. This new alloy design strategy can be readily adapted to large-scale industrial production of HEAs with simultaneous high fracture strength and high ductility.

Moreover, the safety and advancement of modern technologies not only strongly relies on current mechanical properties of these eutectic alloys, but also calls for better ones. To date, many conventional routes to optimize eutectic alloys, such as processing to create line defects, usually result in reduced ductility. Previous studies showed that engineering an ultrafine-grained duplex microstructure by severe cold-rolling and annealing could dramatically strengthen eutectic alloys although degrading ductility. Recently, Wu et al. developed a heterogeneous structure of bimodal grains in Ti, which possesses < 30 vol.% soft, coarse-grained lamellae embedded in a hard, ultrafine-grained lamella matrix,. The resulting materials exhibited great ductility, as a high density of lamella interfaces could induce the building of large strain gradients across them during deformation. Meanwhile, the full deformation constraint imposed by the hard lamella matrix enables the soft lamellae to be almost as strong as the hard matrix, thus making materials with high strength,. decision.trend: Early work on eutectic high-entropy alloys, such as in PMC4145285, focused on designing dual-phase lamellar microstructures by alloy design to achieve a combination of soft and hard phases that inherently balance strength and ductility. Later studies (PMC6353877 and PMC6687781) introduced thermo‐mechanical processes to refine these lamellar colonies into ultrafine or dual heterogeneous microstructures, which improved strength–ductility synergy by enhancing crack‐arresting mechanisms and promoting strain distribution. However, even with these advances, the intrinsic issue of numerous internal boundaries acting as microcrack nucleation sites under room-temperature tension remains.
decision.unsolved: The key challenge persists in that while modifications to the overall microstructure can raise strength, the inherent lamellar interfaces continue to serve as weak spots that trigger early microcracking, thereby limiting ductility. No single intervention so far has directly addressed the intrinsic weakness at these boundaries without compromising other properties.
decision.lever: Tailored low‐temperature annealing to promote in situ interfacial segregation and ordering
decision.why: Building on the trend, where overall microstructural refinement failed to fully eliminate microcrack initiation at internal boundaries, the next plausible step is to directly strengthen these interfaces. A controlled, low‐temperature anneal could drive selective segregation or ordering at the lamellar boundaries without changing the bulk composition, thereby increasing their cohesion. This intervention directly targets microcrack nucleation sites, and prior work showing the benefits of dual heterogeneous structures for crack arrest supports that enhancing interface robustness can improve both strength and ductility. The hypothesis is testable by comparing tensile properties and damage evolution in samples with and without the interfacial treatment under room-temperature deformation.
